## 0, 0.3, 0.30000000000000004

```
0
0.3
0.30000000000000004
```

Three lines that together make the whole point:

1. **`sum == 0.3` is false**, printed as `0`.
2. **`sum` prints as `0.3`** with the default precision, so it *looks* equal.
3. **At 17 digits it is `0.30000000000000004`**, which is why it is not.

The second line is the dangerous one. The default output hides the difference, so the program appears to be working right up until something compares two values.

## Why it happens

A `double` stores a number in **binary**, as a sign, an exponent and a 52-bit fraction. The values it can represent exactly are sums of powers of two. `0.1` is not one of them — writing it in binary gives a repeating pattern:

```
0.1 decimal = 0.0001100110011001100...  binary, forever
```

exactly as one third is `0.333...` in decimal and cannot be written down. So `0.1` is stored as the nearest representable double, which is slightly more than a tenth. Same for `0.2`. Adding the two approximations gives a result whose nearest double is **not** the nearest double to `0.3`.

The errors are tiny — about 5.5e-17 here — and they do not cancel.

## This is not a C++ problem

Every language using IEEE 754 doubles does this, which is almost all of them:

```python
>>> 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3
False
```

```javascript
> 0.1 + 0.2
0.30000000000000004
```

It is a property of binary floating point, not a defect in any one language. Hardware is the same everywhere; `float.exposed` will show you the bits of any value.

## What to do instead of `==`

**Compare with a tolerance.** The naive form:

```cpp
if (std::abs(a - b) < 1e-9) { ... }     // absolute tolerance
```

which is fine when you know the magnitudes. It is wrong when you do not: `1e-9` is a huge tolerance for values near `1e-12` and far too tight for values near `1e12`. The better form scales:

```cpp
#include <cmath>
#include <algorithm>

bool close(double a, double b, double rel = 1e-9)
{
    return std::abs(a - b) <= rel * std::max(std::abs(a), std::abs(b));
}
```

**Do not accumulate.** Adding a million small floats one at a time accumulates error proportional to the number of additions. Summing in pairs (or Kahan summation) keeps it to roughly the square root of that.

**Use an integer when the quantity is discrete.** Money is the classic: store pence as `int`, not pounds as `double`. `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3` is an accounting bug waiting to happen, and every financial system stores integers or a decimal type for this reason.

## Two values that are not equal to themselves

Worth knowing now so it does not surprise you later:

```cpp
double nan{ 0.0 / 0.0 };
std::cout << (nan == nan) << '\n';    // 0 — NaN is not equal to anything, including itself
```

That is deliberate in IEEE 754, and it means `std::sort` on data containing NaN is undefined behaviour, because the comparison is not a valid ordering.

## Printing them honestly

```cpp
#include <iomanip>
std::cout << std::setprecision(17) << sum << '\n';
```

`17` is the magic number: it is the fewest decimal digits that can round-trip any `double` exactly. `std::numeric_limits<double>::max_digits10` is that 17, spelled portably.
